taxonomyNote: NatureServe (following SSAR 2025) restricts L. triangulum to the eastern populations and treats L. gentilis as separate; Chambers et al. (2023) argue for lumping, and Animal Diversity Web describes L. triangulum with 25 subspecies.
fieldMarks: Gray or tan body with a light Y- or V-shaped patch on the neck.
Black-bordered brown or rust-red blotches down back and sides.
Typically 60-130 cm in the United States; 19-23 rows of smooth scales and a single anal plate.
No colour difference between the sexes.
behavior: Solitary and secretive; rarely seen in the open by day but often crosses roads at night; mostly nocturnal in hot weather.
Hides under rotting logs and damp trash; hunts rodents around barns and other buildings.
Groups only at hibernation, and may bask in groups just before and after; inactive about November-March in the north.
Eats voles, mice, rats, birds, eggs, lizards and other snakes.
habitat: Forest edges, open woodland, prairies, rocky hillsides, small streams or marshes and farm or suburban areas; hibernates underground or in rock crevices.
range: Southern Minnesota, Michigan, southern Ontario, southern Quebec and southern Maine south to North Carolina and northern Alabama and Georgia; also Mississippi and northeastern Louisiana.
